ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> For /s/-initial words, the roundedness of the upcoming vowel significantly influenced word-identification accuracy after participants had heard only the first 15 ms of /s/, whereas useful information about vowel height and backness emerged after 75 ms for /f/-initial words.

> Participants were instructed to press a button whenever they noticed that they made a speech error.

> For consonant-vowel syllables, Lackner and Tuller (1979) found that when auditory feedback was masked, participants were somewhat less accurate in detecting place-of-articulation errors (e.g., saying [ti] instead of [pi]), but substantially worse at detecting voicing errors (e.g., saying [bi] instead of [pi]) than when auditory feedback was available.

> In a task where participants are instructed to interrupt utterances when the feedback relays a different word from the one they are producing, would they interrupt an utterance of, for example, best while hearing bend more rapidly when the feedback contains the natural anticipatory coarticulatory cues of bend than when its initial vowel material is cross-spliced from best?

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Portions of the theoretical account developed in this article were presented as a talk at Interdisciplinary Voice 2026, University of York, July 2026.

ChatGPT Edu (OpenAI, 2026), provided through Lund University, was used during preparation of this manuscript to assist with verifying and reviewing the use of cited literature, critically evaluating arguments, and editing and refining the text.
The authors independently evaluated the relevant source literature, reviewed and revised all AI-assisted content, and take full responsibility for the content of the manuscript.

Spontaneous speech is full of false starts, rephrasing, and speech errors.
How do we recognize the need to clarify or reword our own utterances, and how do we know when we make errors?

Many theories assume that some pre-articulatory representation, production state, or derivative prediction-originating in the production process-provides information against which the utterance can be monitored (e.g., Hickok, 2012 Hickok, , 2014;; Levelt, 1989; Levelt et al., 1999; Pickering & Garrod, 2013).
text.formatted: Many theories assume that some pre-articulatory representation, production state, or derivative prediction-originating in the production process-provides information against which the utterance can be monitored (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Hickok, 2012</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Hickok, , 2014;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b124">Levelt, 1989;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b126">Levelt et al., 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b192">Pickering & Garrod, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: But if speech is a fundamentally interactive endeavor, in which our utterances and their meanings are inherently contextually anchored and emerge as speech unfolds, there is reason to question whether pre-articulatory information can provide a sufficiently specified basis for evaluating our own speech.

This paper develops a theory of verbal self-monitoring that is grounded in a framework we propose for addressing the wider question of how we as speakers dynamically determine what we ourselves are saying as speech and interaction unfold.

The assumption that sufficiently specified information about what we are going to say is available before articulation-as instantiated in notions such as speech intentions, prelinguistic messages, or production commands-raises questions about the ontology of such pre-articulatory states, and their content is challenging to study empirically. Dennett (1991) warned against the (often tacit and unknowing) positing of central executives-or overly powerful homunculi-to explain complex cognitive processes.
text.formatted: The assumption that sufficiently specified information about what we are going to say is available before articulation-as instantiated in notions such as speech intentions, prelinguistic messages, or production commands-raises questions about the ontology of such pre-articulatory states, and their content is challenging to study empirically. <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Dennett (1991)</ref> warned against the (often tacit and unknowing) positing of central executives-or overly powerful homunculi-to explain complex cognitive processes.

text.text: In relation to speech production, Dennett (1991) criticized what he called the illusion of the Central Meaner, or the idea that all the intricate processes that result in words being spoken can be reduced to a single point of origin.
text.formatted: In relation to speech production, <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Dennett (1991)</ref> criticized what he called the illusion of the Central Meaner, or the idea that all the intricate processes that result in words being spoken can be reduced to a single point of origin.

text.text: Focusing particularly on Levelt's (1989) Conceptualizer as an example of this problem, Dennett (1991) noted that it has access to all the speaker's knowledge, memory, and plans, and produces pre-verbal messages that constrain the meaning and subsequent formulation of the overt utterance.
text.formatted: Focusing particularly on <ref type="bibr" target="#b124">Levelt's (1989)</ref> Conceptualizer as an example of this problem, <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Dennett (1991)</ref> noted that it has access to all the speaker's knowledge, memory, and plans, and produces pre-verbal messages that constrain the meaning and subsequent formulation of the overt utterance.

text.text: Moreover, for Levelt, the Conceptualizer is also the seat of the monitor, and the original message ultimately provides a criterion against which the appropriateness of the resulting utterance can be evaluated.

While Levelt explicitly acknowledges that the Conceptualizer is a functional abstraction encompassing disparate cognitive processes that ultimately need to be unpacked, he leaves that unpacking outside the scope of his theory. Dennett's (1991) concern is that this abstraction is assigned precisely the capacity for message generation and monitoring that requires explanation.
text.formatted: While Levelt explicitly acknowledges that the Conceptualizer is a functional abstraction encompassing disparate cognitive processes that ultimately need to be unpacked, he leaves that unpacking outside the scope of his theory. <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Dennett's (1991)</ref> concern is that this abstraction is assigned precisely the capacity for message generation and monitoring that requires explanation.

text.text: Many theories of verbal self-monitoring similarly treat message generation as abstract-or outside the explanatory scope-while nevertheless making monitoring dependent on information generated through the production process.

Although the information made available to monitoring differs between theories-e.g., conflict during lexical or phonological selection in Nozari et al. (2011), sensory targets and predictions in Hickok (2012 Hickok ( , 2014)), and predictions generated from an efference copy of a production command in Pickering and Garrod (2013)-monitoring is consequently conceived as downstream of and tightly coupled with the production process.

(2011)</ref>, sensory targets and predictions in <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Hickok (2012</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Hickok ( , 2014))</ref>, and predictions generated from an efference copy of a production command in <ref type="bibr" target="#b192">Pickering and Garrod (2013)</ref>-monitoring is consequently conceived as downstream of and tightly coupled with the production process.

text.text: A related challenge to assumptions about the pre-articulatory specification of upcoming speech comes from Linell (e.g., 1979 Linell (e.g., , 1998 Linell (e.g., , 2009)), who emphasizes the intrinsically interactional nature of speech and criticizes the view of the speaker as a fully autonomous subject.
text.formatted: A related challenge to assumptions about the pre-articulatory specification of upcoming speech comes from <ref type="bibr">Linell (e.g., 1979</ref> <ref type="bibr">Linell (e.g., , 1998</ref> <ref type="bibr">Linell (e.g., , 2009))</ref>, who emphasizes the intrinsically interactional nature of speech and criticizes the view of the speaker as a fully autonomous subject.

text.text: Instead, Linell proposes that speakers are interdependent with others, that cognition and communication are inseparably connected, and that, consequently, an utterance's broader meaning and significance do not originate solely in the speaker's mind, but emerge through interaction between the speaker, interlocutors, and the unique communicative context.
Therefore, the speaker cannot be assumed to know the full meaning and significance of their own utterance prior to speaking.
Instead, meaning is progressively specified-for the speaker-as the utterance unfolds and they hear their own voice and perceive both their own reactions and those of their interlocutors.
As Dennett (1991) put it: "… the speaker gets no preview; he and his audience learn what the speaker's utterance is at the same time" (p. 238).
text.formatted: As <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Dennett (1991)</ref> put it: "… the speaker gets no preview; he and his audience learn what the speaker's utterance is at the same time" (p. 238).

text.text: We have previously investigated the idea that speakers use sensory feedback from their own speech to comprehend and make sense of what they themselves are saying.

In Lind et al. (2014a), we created a mismatch between what speakers said and the auditory feedback they received, thereby also creating a putative mismatch between the feedback and whatever pre-articulatory information had guided the utterance.
text.formatted: In <ref type="bibr">Lind et al. (2014a)</ref>, we created a mismatch between what speakers said and the auditory feedback they received, thereby also creating a putative mismatch between the feedback and whatever pre-articulatory information had guided the utterance.

text.text: Speaking into specially constructed sound-isolating headsets while performing a Stroop test, participants' utterances (e.g., green) were sometimes surreptitiously recorded.
Using a precise sound trigger mechanism, the recordings were later inserted into speakers' auditory feedback while feedback from what they said (e.g., gray) was blocked.

Participants often believed that they had uttered the inserted word, demonstrating that auditory feedback can substantially influence speakers' judgments about what they themselves have said (see Meekings et al., 2015, and Lind et al., 2015, for discussion).

text.text: Based on these findings, we proposed the selfcomprehension hypothesis: that speakers use sensory feedback from their own speech as a source of information about what they themselves are saying (Lind et al., 2014b).
text.formatted: Based on these findings, we proposed the selfcomprehension hypothesis: that speakers use sensory feedback from their own speech as a source of information about what they themselves are saying <ref type="bibr" target="#b129">(Lind et al., 2014b)</ref>.

text.text: We further proposed that verbal error monitoring has a strong cue-integrative 1 character: rather than determining if what one has said was correct with reference to privileged pre-articulatory representations, judgments about appropriateness and correctness are instead shaped by multiple cues from sensory and contextual information (Lind et al., 2014a (Lind et al., , 2014b)).
text.formatted: We further proposed that verbal error monitoring has a strong cue-integrative 1 character: rather than determining if what one has said was correct with reference to privileged pre-articulatory representations, judgments about appropriateness and correctness are instead shaped by multiple cues from sensory and contextual information <ref type="bibr">(Lind et al., 2014a</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b129">(Lind et al., , 2014b))</ref>.

text.text: In the present paper, we develop our account of how speech errors and other problems can be detected within the self-comprehension model.

2 Sensory feedback is a natural candidate for playing a prominent role in this account because it is clearly available to the speaker, even if no other assumptions are made about the speech production system.
Speaking generates several forms of sensory feedback.

Self-produced sound reaches the auditory system through both air and bone conduction, while somatosensory signals convey information about the configuration and movement of the articulators as well as contacts between oral surfaces (e.g., Lackner & Tuller, 1979; Postma, 2000; Kent, 2024; Lind &   1 In Lind et al. (2014b) we used the term inferential.

(2014b)</ref> we used the term inferential.

text.text: We now prefer cue-integrative because inferential can suggest a discrete process that explicitly performs an inference, whereas the proposed account seeks to describe the emergent integration of multiple contextual and sensorimotor cues.
2 We do not attempt to explain how or why errors arise.

The self-comprehension model does not depend on a particular account of how errors are generated, and it does not require the processes responsible for generating an error to also provide the mechanism by which that error is detected.
Rather, it concerns how information in the unfolding utterance can allow them to be detected.

Although we use conventionally transcribed speech errors as examples throughout the paper, such transcriptions should not be taken to imply that errors necessarily involve categorical substitutions or transpositions of discrete speech units.

Articulatory and acoustic studies have shown that apparent errors can involve gradient, overlapping, or co-produced articulatory patterns (e.g., Boucher, 1994; Goldstein et al., 2007; Mowrey & MacKay, 1990; Pouplier, 2007; Pouplier & Goldstein, 2010), with gradient phonetic effects also observed in spontaneous speech errors (Alderete et al., 2021). Hartsuiker, 2020).

text.text: However, two problems must be addressed if sensory feedback is to play a central role in error-detection.

First, if self-monitoring does not rely on access to sufficiently specified pre-articulatory information, and if speakers determine what they themselves are saying through self-comprehension as the utterance unfolds, how can they distinguish feedback indicating a speech error or communicative problem from feedback indicating an appropriate utterance?

Second, assumptions about substantial processing delays in the use of sensory feedback have led many accounts of speech monitoring to conclude that sensory feedback cannot explain the many error interruptions that are made faster than those delays would allow.

Consequently, different monitoring mechanisms relying on information from speech planning processes-including internally perceived phonological representations (e.g., Levelt et al., 1999; Wheeldon & Levelt, 1995), predictions (e.g., Hickok, 2012 Hickok, , 2014;; Pickering & Garrod, 2013), and conflict within lexical or phonological selection processes (Nozari et al., 2011)-have been proposed to account for such swift interruptions.
text.formatted: Consequently, different monitoring mechanisms relying on information from speech planning processes-including internally perceived phonological representations (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b126">Levelt et al., 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b252">Wheeldon & Levelt, 1995)</ref>, predictions (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Hickok, 2012</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Hickok, , 2014;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b192">Pickering & Garrod, 2013)</ref>, and conflict within lexical or phonological selection processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b176">(Nozari et al., 2011)</ref>-have been proposed to account for such swift interruptions.

text.text: The present paper therefore centers on two questions: How can speakers determine that their unfolding speech is erroneous or otherwise problematic without requiring privileged monitoring access to pre-articulatory production representations?
And how can sensory feedback become informative rapidly enough to contribute to the detection of even very quickly interrupted errors?
We suggest that verbal self-monitoring is a natural sub-function of selfcomprehension.
We propose no mechanism developed specifically for self-monitoring; rather, speakers sometimes detect errors and other problems in the course of comprehending their own speech.

Like speech comprehension more generally, selfcomprehension is a multilevel, cue-integrative process in which available contextual, linguistic, and sensory information can jointly constrain the interpretation of unfolding speech.
Importantly, these sources of information need not operate independently.

Through speech production and learning, systematic relationships develop among speech representations and the auditory, somatosensory, and motor states associated with speaking (e.g., Franken et al., 2022; Guenther & Vladusich, 2012; Ito et al., 2016; Lametti et al., 2012; Nasir & Ostry, 2009).
text.formatted: Through speech production and learning, systematic relationships develop among speech representations and the auditory, somatosensory, and motor states associated with speaking (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Franken et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Guenther & Vladusich, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">Ito et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b122">Lametti et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b170">Nasir & Ostry, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: We propose that these learned relationships provide a basis for interactions between speech and sensory information during self-comprehension.
3   Within this cue-integrative system, we propose that two sources of anticipatory information are particularly important for self-comprehension and self-monitoring.

The first is multi-scale pattern completion (MSPC), proposed by Falandays et al. (2021) as a mechanism capable of producing prediction-like anticipatory activation during language comprehension without requiring explicitly predictive representations, and here extended to self-comprehension.
text.formatted: The first is multi-scale pattern completion (MSPC), proposed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Falandays et al. (2021)</ref> as a mechanism capable of producing prediction-like anticipatory activation during language comprehension without requiring explicitly predictive representations, and here extended to self-comprehension.

text.text: The second is anticipatory sensory information generated by the speaker's own unfolding articulation, particularly information arising from auditory and somatosensory coarticulation.

Auditory coarticulatory cues are well established as a source of anticipatory information during other-comprehension (e.g., Beddor et al., 2013; Gow & McMurray, 2007; Salverda et al., 2014; Schreiber & McMurray, 2019), and recent work has proposed that speakers may use early sensory consequences of anticipatory coarticulation for speech control (Floegel et al., 2023; Kasper et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Auditory coarticulatory cues are well established as a source of anticipatory information during other-comprehension (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Beddor et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Gow & McMurray, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b218">Salverda et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b223">Schreiber & McMurray, 2019)</ref>, and recent work has proposed that speakers may use early sensory consequences of anticipatory coarticulation for speech control <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Floegel et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b107">Kasper et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: We suggest that anticipatory coarticulatory information in both auditory and somatosensory feedback can also contribute to self-comprehension by constraining speakers' interpretation of their own unfolding speech.

Because coarticulatory information about upcoming speech can become available before the relevant speech segment is articulated, sensory information may become informative substantially earlier than assumed by accounts that estimate monitoring latency from post-articulatory feedback alone.
We propose that upcoming errors can likewise be reflected, at least partly, in this anticipatory coarticulatory information.

MSPC can support anticipatory activation at multiple linguistic levels, whereas coarticulatory sensory information provides particularly early constraints on the articulatory and phonological properties of upcoming speech.

3 Production-related motor and somatosensory information constraining self-comprehension should not be confused with privileged monitoring access to a representation specifying the intended utterance.

On the present account, these states provide additional constraints on cue-integrative self-comprehension; they do not independently specify the intended utterance or provide a criterion of correctness.
circumstances will, on average, be associated with progressively longer-but partly overlapping-error interruption latencies.

The swiftest interruptions should be most likely when MSPC provides a sufficiently strong and specific anticipation and informative coarticulatory sensory cues diverge from it sufficiently early to signal an emerging problem.

When such anticipatory information is unavailable, inadequately informative, or insufficiently divergent, error detection will depend increasingly on post-articulatory sensory information and its integration with the wider linguistic and communicative context.

Detection latency will therefore depend not only on which sources of information are available, but also on when they become informative and how strongly and unambiguously they constrain selfcomprehension.

This account is therefore capable, in principle, of accommodating error interruptions across the empirically observed distribution of error-to-cutoff times (Blackmer & Mitton, 1991; Hartsuiker & Kolk, 2001; Levelt, 1983).

text.text: Speech comprehension is widely thought to involve anticipatory processing based on recent speech context (e.g., Kuperberg & Jaeger, 2016; Pickering & Gambi, 2018).

text.text: Such anticipatory processing is often interpreted as evidence that listeners predict upcoming speech.

For example, in a classic study, Altmann and Kamide (1999) showed that eye movements toward an image of a cake began prior to the onset of the word cake when participants heard the sentence "the boy will eat the cake," but only after the onset of cake when the verb was instead move, showing that sentence context can lead listeners to anticipate upcoming speech.

(2021) draw on research in visual perception documenting both perceptual completion, whereby occluded or otherwise incompletely visible stimuli can nevertheless be perceived as complete (e.g., Grossberg, 2003; Mendola, 2003; Weil & Rees, 2011), and forward-looking perceptual effects, such as representational momentum, whereby objects that disappear while moving are judged or remembered as having progressed slightly farther along their trajectory than their actual final position (e.g., Freyd, 1987; Freyd & Finke, 1984; Jordan & Hunsinger, 2008). text.text: Because these representations reflect learned regularities in experience, the resulting pattern completion is inherently context-sensitive: the particular state activated at one moment constrains which states are partially activated next.
As Falandays et al. (2021) put it, these learned patterns allow the organism to "'lean […] forward in time' with a kind of momentum that, to an outside observer, resembles prediction" (p. 4).
text.formatted: As <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Falandays et al. (2021)</ref> put it, these learned patterns allow the organism to "'lean <ref type="bibr">[…]</ref> forward in time' with a kind of momentum that, to an outside observer, resembles prediction" (p. 4).

text.text: For humans, these learned regularities include the temporal structure of language.

text.text: When jTRACE receives only an initial fragment of a word-Falandays et al. (2021) use, for example, /əda/ from adapt and /prɑg/ from progress-activation at the lexical level feeds back to phoneme units corresponding to portions of the word that have not yet occurred in the input.
The model therefore partially activates upcoming phonological information on the basis of incomplete input.
Thus, multi-level pattern completion produces anticipatory activation of upcoming phonemes without explicit representations of predictions or prediction errors.

Second, Falandays et al. (2021) present a simplified homeostatic reservoir model demonstrating that prediction-like behavior can emerge through unsupervised learning.

text.text: The model consists of interconnected nodes whose coupling strengths and target activity adapt locally in pursuit of homeostasis.

After exposure to simple probabilistic sequences, the network's "fading memory" activity following the removal of external input tends to resemble the population code for the input that would have been most likely to occur next.

This activity is sensitive not only to local transition probabilities but also to the temporal position of an input and the overall probability of the sequence in which it occurs, indicating that the network has become sensitive to temporal structure rather than merely to individual input patterns. Falandays et al. (2021) explain this pattern-completion behavior as arising because the network increasingly depends on its own internally generated activity: when external input ceases, the preceding activity pattern continues to drive nodes associated with likely upcoming input.

text.text: Thus, prediction-like behavior emerges from the learned dynamics of the system without explicit predictive representations or prediction-error computation.

Taken together, Falandays et al.'s (2021) arguments and computational demonstrations show how prediction-like anticipatory processing can emerge through temporally forward-reaching pattern completion.

text.text: We suggest that the same general principle of MSPC can operate during self-comprehension.
Crucially, the information driving MSPC during self-comprehension need not originate in a representation of the speaker's intended utterance.
As in other-comprehension, preceding linguistic and communicative context can activate learned continuations at multiple levels.
During selfcomprehension, the speaker's own previously produced speech forms part of this unfolding context, together with the wider discourse and communicative situation.

We therefore propose that, as speakers comprehend their own unfolding speech, MSPC can generate anticipatory activation 5 at phonological, lexical, syntactic, and semantic levels on the basis of the linguistic and communicative context.
Such anticipatory activation does not require a separate explicit representation of the predicted future input.

Importantly, the resulting anticipation differs from the production-derived predictions proposed in forward-model accounts: rather than stemming from, for example, an efference copy, it is generated from the kinds of contextual regularities that also support anticipation during othercomprehension.
MSPC thus provides one source of anticipatory information during selfcomprehension.

We next consider a second-anticipatory sensory information arising from coarticulation-and how such information may allow sensory feedback to become informative earlier than is commonly assumed in accounts of speech monitoring.
Sensory feedback has long been proposed to play a central role in verbal selfmonitoring (e.g., Levelt, 1989; Levelt et al., 1999; Pickering & Garrod, 2013; but see Nozari et al., 2011; Nozari, 2018).
text.formatted: Sensory feedback has long been proposed to play a central role in verbal selfmonitoring (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b124">Levelt, 1989;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b126">Levelt et al., 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b192">Pickering & Garrod, 2013</ref>; but see <ref type="bibr" target="#b176">Nozari et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b174">Nozari, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: However, sensory feedback has often been considered too slow to account for the most rapid instances of error detection and interruption, motivating the proposal of faster, pre-articulatory monitoring mechanisms.

Yet acoustic analyses of anticipatory coarticulation suggest that this assumption warrants reconsideration: acoustic information about upcoming speech can become available well before the onset of the relevant speech segment (e.g., Salverda et al., 2014; Schreiber & McMurray, 2019). Floegel et al. (2023) introduced an informational account in which anticipatory coarticulation may provide speakers with advance information about their own upcoming speech that can be used to control ongoing speech production, an account subsequently developed and empirically investigated by Kasper et al. (2026).

text.text: Crucially, Kasper et al. (2026) argued that the early availability of such information challenges the common assumption that sensory feedback is necessarily too slow for direct use in speech control.

text.text: We extend this proposal to self-comprehension and speech-error monitoring, suggesting that speakers may exploit anticipatory sensory information generated through coarticulation to constrain their interpretation of their own unfolding speech.

A related possibility was raised much earlier by Postma and Kolk (1992;  see their footnote 3), who considered whether speakers might use acoustic coarticulatory cues to anticipate upcoming speech errors, thereby potentially accounting for rapid error interruptions without recourse to internal monitoring.

text.text: Although they were skeptical that "such subtle acoustic information" (p. 542) could be used during verbal self-monitoring, subsequent research, reviewed below, prompts renewed consideration of this possibility.
The present proposal additionally considers anticipatory information available through somatosensory coarticulation.

If speakers exploit such auditory and somatosensory anticipatory information during self-comprehension, sensory feedback may become informative about an upcoming speech error substantially earlier than has generally been assumed, changing the temporal constraints traditionally attributed to sensory-feedbackbased speech monitoring.

We first examine the origins of these commonly assumed temporal constraints and then review the observed distribution of error-interruption latencies, including the rapid interruptions that have motivated proposals for pre-articulatory monitoring.

Based on speech shadowing and word-monitoring studies (Marslen-Wilson, 1973; Marslen-Wilson & Tyler, 1980), Marslen-Wilson and Tyler (1981) estimated that words in utterance contexts can typically be recognized within approximately 200 ms of word onset. Levelt (1989) subsequently applied this estimate to the external monitoring of self-produced speech, treating approximately 200 ms as the minimum time required to detect an error through the auditory perceptual loop. Hartsuiker and Kolk (2001) further argued that the perceptual latency should be supplemented by the time required to implement an interruption once an error has been detected.

On the basis of approximately 200-ms stopping latencies in externally cued interruption tasks involving speech (Ladefoged et al., 1973) and finger movements (Logan & Cowan, 1984), and subtracting an estimated 50 ms for perception of the stop signal, Hartsuiker and Kolk (2001) arrived at an interruptionimplementation latency of approximately 150 ms.

text.text: As suggested above, however, sensory information about upcoming speech can become available substantially earlier than has generally been assumed.

We therefore propose that such early sensory information can contribute to self-monitoring; if so, rapid error interruptions would no longer, by themselves, require the postulation of a prearticulatory monitoring channel.
To address this possibility, we first review research demonstrating that acoustic coarticulatory cues allow listeners to anticipate upcoming speech.

We then review evidence that articulatory movements themselves contain extensive anticipatory information about upcoming speech, which is potentially available to the speaker through somatosensory feedback.

Crucially, we propose that these auditory and somatosensory cues are used by speakers during self-comprehension to anticipate upcoming properties of their own utterances, thereby sometimes allowing sensory information to contribute to self-comprehension substantially earlier than has generally been assumed.
Finally, we review evidence suggesting that the error-interruption implementation latency may be considerably shorter than previously estimated.
As reviewed above, the approximately 200-ms estimate derived from spoken-word recognition was subsequently applied to the temporal constraints on auditory self-monitoring.

However, it has long been established that listeners can use acoustic coarticulatory information in preceding speech to anticipate upcoming speech (e.g., Fowler, 1984; Gow, 2001; Martin & Bunnell, 1982; Sereno et al., 1987; Warren & Marslen-Wilson, 1987 , 1988; Whalen, 1984; Yeni-Komshian & Soli, 1981), and more recent studies examining the precise time course with which such information can influence speech comprehension suggest very early effects.

text.text: Following the same logic outlined above of applying findings from othercomprehension to self-comprehension and self-monitoring, we therefore propose that speakers use coarticulatory information during self-comprehension as well.

We focus here on studies that reveal how early such coarticulatory information can influence spokenlanguage comprehension and the temporal advantage it can provide relative to target onset. Gow and McMurray (2007) investigated the between-word effects of coronal place assimilation, in which a word-final coronal consonant takes on place-of-articulation properties of a following word-initial non-coronal consonant, so that, for example, green boat is pronounced as greem boat.

text.text: Across two experiments, participants heard utterances such as "the ladder is the target." n the first experiment, coarticulatory information was removed by splicing a token of the definite article produced in a neutral context into the sentence initial position and adding a brief pause after it (e.g., "the… ladder is the target"). n the second experiment, the determiner and target word were naturally produced as a single phonological phrase and contained the relevant coarticulatory cues.
When anticipatory coarticulation was absent, the earliest languagedirected saccades were initiated within 200-240 ms after target-word onset.

When it was available, however, the earliest saccades were launched approximately 70 ms earlier, in the 130-170 ms window, with marginal effects already evident in the 110-150 ms and 120-160 ms windows. Salverda et al. (2014) noted that this temporal advantage corresponded closely to the duration of the preceding determiner vowel (M = 53 ms, range = 30-78 ms).

text.text: Furthermore, examination of the formant structure of the determiner vowel showed that potentially informative coarticulatory cues about the upcoming speech sound were present very early, within approximately the first 10-20 ms of the vowel.

Together, these findings show that anticipatory coarticulatory information about the upcoming word was available very early in the preceding segment and that listeners could exploit this to gain a substantial temporal advantage in spoken-word processing.

When nasalization distinguished the target from the competitor, participants looked at the target significantly earlier when nasalization began early rather than late in the vowel, with an advantage of approximately 20-40 ms for early nasalization.

Across items, divergence between target and competitor fixations began approximately 240-250 ms after the onset of vowel nasalization, with the difference becoming significant at approximately 260-270 ms.

Assuming an approximately 200-ms eye-movement programming latency, these results indicate that listeners can exploit anticipatory coarticulatory nasalization very rapidly after it becomes available, well before the onset of the nasal consonant, and, crucially, that the timing of perceptual processing can vary with the timing of the coarticulatory information in the speech signal.

text.text: The fricatives had a mean duration of 264 ms, and acoustic analysis showed that coarticulatory cues to the upcoming vowel were present within the first ~50 ms of the fricative.

The coarticulatory manipulation produced a divergence in fixation patterns already around 30 ms into the subsequent vowel, with participants looking more frequently toward the object consistent with the vowel anticipated by the coarticulatory cues.

Given an approximately 200-ms latency for planning and launching an eye movement, this indicates that the coarticulatory information had begun influencing processing during the preceding fricative, potentially as early as approximately 170 ms before vowel onset.
Remarkably, listeners were able to use the coarticulatory information to anticipate the upcoming vowel before they had identified the fricative carrying this information.

These findings demonstrate that listeners can begin processing information about an upcoming speech segment well before that segment is heard, and even before the segment carrying the anticipatory information has itself been identified.

Using a gating paradigm, Lulaci et al. (2024) similarly demonstrated that listeners can exploit coarticulatory information about an upcoming vowel from extremely short fragments of a preceding fricative.
text.formatted: Using a gating paradigm, <ref type="bibr" target="#b141">Lulaci et al. (2024)</ref> similarly demonstrated that listeners can exploit coarticulatory information about an upcoming vowel from extremely short fragments of a preceding fricative.

text.text: For /s/-initial words, the roundedness of the upcoming vowel significantly influenced word-identification accuracy after participants had heard only the first 15 ms of /s/, whereas useful information about vowel height and backness emerged after 75 ms for /f/-initial words.

Thus, listeners can exploit anticipatory coarticulatory information about upcoming speech from as little as 15 ms of preceding acoustic input, although the timing with which such information becomes useful varies across speech sounds and articulatory features.
As we saw, Beddor et al. (2013) showed that making coarticulatory information available earlier within a word can lead to earlier effects on comprehension.
text.formatted: As we saw, <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Beddor et al. (2013)</ref> showed that making coarticulatory information available earlier within a word can lead to earlier effects on comprehension.

text.text: There are indications that a similar principle may apply to between-word anticipatory coarticulation as well. Altmann (2011), reanalyzing data from Kamide et al. (2003) and Altmann (2004), found that language-mediated saccades were sometimes initiated as early as 80-120 ms post target-word onset, earlier than in both Gow and McMurray (2007) and Salverda et al. (2014).

(2014)</ref>.

text.text: Assuming an approximately 200-ms saccade-planning latency, this suggests that speech information could have begun guiding saccade planning as early as approximately 120 ms before target-word onset.

Although Altmann (2011) did not analyze coarticulatory information in these stimuli, Salverda et al. (2014) noted that the mean durations of the determiners preceding the target words were substantially longer in Kamide et al. (2003;  176 ms) and Altmann (2004; 170 ms) than in their own stimuli (100 ms; see also Mitterer & Reinisch, 2013).

text.text: One possibility is therefore that the longer determiners allowed relevant coarticulatory information to become available earlier, contributing to the earlier saccades observed in Altmann's (2011) analysis.

text.text: More generally, prolongation of speech segments carrying anticipatory coarticulatory information-for example, in slow or carefully articulated speech or for pragmatic purposes-could potentially increase the temporal advantage afforded by such information.

The studies recounted above show how several different types of coarticulatory cues in various speech segments allow listeners to anticipate upcoming speech both within and between words, with perceptual effects emerging before the onset of the speech segment to which the cues pertain.

Evidence from spontaneous and experimentally elicited speech errors indicates that error-related information penetrates the articulatory implementation of speech and participates in its context-sensitive organization (e.g., Alderete et al., 2021; Goldstein et al., 2007; Slis & Van Lieshout, 2016).
text.formatted: Evidence from spontaneous and experimentally elicited speech errors indicates that error-related information penetrates the articulatory implementation of speech and participates in its context-sensitive organization (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Alderete et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Goldstein et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b229">Slis & Van Lieshout, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: These findings provide a basis for proposing that an upcoming error can be reflected, at least partly, in anticipatory coarticulatory information before the conventional locus of the error.

Following the logic outlined above of applying findings from other-comprehension to self-comprehension and self-monitoring, we propose that speakers similarly use auditory coarticulatory cues during self-comprehension, allowing them to anticipate aspects of their own upcoming speech before the relevant segment is produced.

This proposal converges with Floegel et al.'s (2023) and Kasper et al.'s (2026) proposal that speakers use sensory information arising from anticipatory coarticulation to guide ongoing speech production.
text.formatted: This proposal converges with <ref type="bibr">Floegel et al.'s (2023)</ref> and <ref type="bibr">Kasper et al.'s (2026)</ref> proposal that speakers use sensory information arising from anticipatory coarticulation to guide ongoing speech production.

text.text: Crucially, such anticipatory self-comprehension need not require a separately generated production-derived prediction or privileged monitoring access to pre-articulatory production representations.
Acoustic coarticulatory cues arise from movements and configurations of the articulatory apparatus.

For example, movements of the tongue alter the resonant properties of the vocal tract and hence formant frequencies, whereas lowering of the velum couples the oral and nasal cavities and produces acoustic correlates of nasalization.
Crucially, the articulatory requirements of an upcoming speech sound can begin to reshape the speech apparatus during preceding sounds, sometimes several segments before the target.

These changes also generate somatosensory information, including tactile, proprioceptive, and pressure-related information from the oral, pharyngeal, laryngeal, and respiratory apparatus (Kent, 2024).
text.formatted: These changes also generate somatosensory information, including tactile, proprioceptive, and pressure-related information from the oral, pharyngeal, laryngeal, and respiratory apparatus <ref type="bibr" target="#b110">(Kent, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: There is direct evidence that speech-related somatosensory information can carry phonetic information: speech-like facial skin stretch systematically alters heard phoneme identity (Ito et al., 2009), and speakers can categorize vowels from tongue somatosensation alone, with performance comparable to categorization from whispered speech (Patri et al., 2020).
text.formatted: There is direct evidence that speech-related somatosensory information can carry phonetic information: speech-like facial skin stretch systematically alters heard phoneme identity <ref type="bibr" target="#b100">(Ito et al., 2009)</ref>, and speakers can categorize vowels from tongue somatosensation alone, with performance comparable to categorization from whispered speech <ref type="bibr">(Patri et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Somatosensory information from the speech apparatus can also be processed rapidly.

Unexpected tongue stretch during a speech posture elicits a speechenhanced muscular response at approximately 50 ms, followed by compensatory tongue movement at approximately 130 ms even when auditory feedback is masked (Bourhis et al., 2024; Ito et al., 2024).

text.text: These findings demonstrate that speech-related changes in articulatory state can be registered rapidly through somatosensory feedback.

Anticipatory labial activity associated with an upcoming /u/ has been observed hundreds of milliseconds before the acoustic onset of the vowel (Bell-Berti & Harris, 1979; Perkell & Matthies, 1992), with Bell-Berti and Harris (1979), for example, reporting onsets of approximately 140-290 ms before /u/.

text.text: Anticipatory changes also occur in the pharyngeal walls.

Movement of the superior lateral pharyngeal walls toward the configuration associated with an upcoming nasal began as much as roughly 80 ms before the voice onset of the vowel preceding that nasal-that is, before the preceding vowel's voicing onset (Parush & Ostry, 1986).

text.text: At the lower lateral pharyngeal walls, pharyngeal position during an intervening consonant depended on the identity of the upcoming vowel, with movement away from the configuration for the initial vowel beginning as much as roughly 200 ms before the final vowel's voice onset (Parush & Ostry, 1993).

text.text: Laryngeal preparation can likewise begin well before the supralaryngeal realization of an upcoming consonant.
For intervocalic voiceless stops, posterior cricoarytenoid activity associated with the glottal-opening gesture began approximately 70-160 ms before oral closure (Hirose & Gay, 1972).

text.text: Jaw trajectories can likewise contain information about an upcoming vowel during the movement toward an intervening consonant.
In VCV sequences, the identity and openness of the final vowel affected the amplitude and duration of the initial vowel-to-consonant jawclosing movement (Ostry et al., 1996).

text.text: In this section, we have seen detailed evidence for highly context-sensitive anticipatory coarticulation across multiple articulatory structures, with target-dependent articulatory differences sometimes emerging hundreds of milliseconds before the relevant speech segment.

Consistent with this literature, Kasper et al. (2026) found that articulation during preceding phonemes systematically differed according to the identity of an upcoming phoneme, with effects extending up to approximately 300 ms before its canonical onset in longer vowels and 200 ms in shorter consonants.

(2026)</ref> found that articulation during preceding phonemes systematically differed according to the identity of an upcoming phoneme, with effects extending up to approximately 300 ms before its canonical onset in longer vowels and 200 ms in shorter consonants.

text.text: Together, these findings establish that target-dependent articulatory differences capable of generating potentially informative somatosensory feedback can emerge well before the speech segments to which they pertain. Kasper et al. (2026) propose that speakers use such early sensory information to control ongoing speech, although their study did not directly test its use.

text.text: We extend this proposal to self-comprehension, hypothesizing that anticipatory somatosensory coarticulatory information constrains speakers' interpretation of their own upcoming speech.

Together with coarticulatory cues in the auditory modality, such information could diverge from MSPC-based anticipation and thereby provide a cue that the unfolding utterance is problematic or constitutes a speech error before the relevant speech segment has been articulated.
How quickly can an interruption be implemented once some error signal is processed?

As we have seen, the previously proposed ~150 ms interruption implementation latency for speech was derived by Hartsuiker and Kolk (2001) from stop-signal studies by Ladefoged et al. (1973) and Logan and Cowan (1984).

(1973)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b138">Logan and Cowan (1984)</ref>.

text.text: There is, however, evidence that events registered by somatosensory and auditory feedback can elicit relevant responses much more rapidly.

Mechanical perturbations to speech articulators can elicit task-specific compensatory responses within tens of milliseconds (e.g., Gracco & Abbs, 1985; Kelso et al., 1984; see Grimme et al., 2011; Kent, 2024, for reviews).

text.text: As mentioned above, neither tone-prompted interruptions nor somatosensory or auditory responses to perturbed feedback provide a perfect analogy to interrupting erroneous speech-empirical work is needed.

We therefore emphasize that, as will be clear in the following sections, even if the error-interruption implementation latency is in fact approximately 150 ms, as Hartsuiker and Kolk (2001) proposed, speech could still be interrupted, for example, 50 ms after error onset if anticipatory coarticulatory information allowed the error to be detected 100 ms before its onset.

text.text: We next consider how MSPCbased anticipation and auditory and somatosensory information from the unfolding utterance-including anticipatory information arising from coarticulation-may contribute to the detection and interruption of speech errors.

We have seen how anticipations based on MSPC and on coarticulatory cues can activate knowledge at the phonological and lexical levels very rapidly, and we have argued that these anticipations are also integral to verbal self-comprehension and self-monitoring.
Before detailing how error monitoring may operate in the self-comprehension model, we again emphasize that self-comprehension is likely not achieved through a single mechanism or process.
Rather, the context will dictate what information-including anticipatory cues-is available to the speaker, and when it is available.

For example, Huettig and Mani (2016; see also Pickering & Gambi, 2018) reviewed the available data on prediction during speech comprehension and questioned the view that prediction is an inherent and ubiquitous aspect of human cognition (e.g., Clark, 2013; Friston, 2005) and of language processing.
text.formatted: For example, Huettig and Mani (2016; see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b191">Pickering & Gambi, 2018)</ref> reviewed the available data on prediction during speech comprehension and questioned the view that prediction is an inherent and ubiquitous aspect of human cognition (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Clark, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Friston, 2005)</ref> and of language processing.

text.text: Instead, Huettig and Mani (2016) argued that prediction-which, following Falandays et al. (2021), can on the present account be reconceptualized as MSPC-based anticipation-does not appear to be necessary for language comprehension, with some individuals appearing not to use it under conditions in which others do.
text.formatted: Instead, <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">Huettig and Mani (2016)</ref> argued that prediction-which, following <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Falandays et al. (2021)</ref>, can on the present account be reconceptualized as MSPC-based anticipation-does not appear to be necessary for language comprehension, with some individuals appearing not to use it under conditions in which others do.

text.text: Rather, prediction can be used opportunistically when there are strong enough contextual cues, and enough cognitive resources, such as working memory. Huettig and Mani (2016) concluded by stating that "[s]ometimes, processing words when they occur may be more efficient and economical than predicting them" (p. 28).

text.text: Moreover, the available evidence suggests that anticipatory processing based on MSPC and coarticulation may generally provide weaker or less sustained constraints than post-articulatory speech comprehension (i.e., "processing words when they occur"). Falandays et al. (2021) showed that phonemes anticipated via MSPC receive partial activation in the absence of corresponding bottom-up input. text.text: We suggest that these observations apply to MSPC-and coarticulation-based anticipations and post-articulatory processing during self-comprehension as well: anticipatory processing can be highly informative when it is available, but it is not necessary, and post-articulatory selfcomprehension is likely often more efficient, precise, and certain-but slower.

This suggests that, while errors are sometimes detected and interrupted rapidly based on anticipatory cues, many errors will be detected and interrupted later, via postarticulatory self-comprehension.

text.text: Quicker interruptions, we suggest, arise primarily through route (a), while progressively slower interruptions arise primarily through routes (b) and (c) (although, as discussed further below, there is unlikely to be a hard temporal dividing line between interruption latencies of errors detected based on (a), (b), or (c) 10 ).
In the following sections, we will spell out routes (a)-(c) in detail, focusing on their temporal implications.

We suggest that anticipatory somatosensory and auditory coarticulatory cues provide rapidly available information about upcoming speech that can reveal a mismatch between the developing utterance and the anticipation generated by MSPC, potentially allowing rapid error detection.
We illustrate this principle with Levelt's (1983) "… is a [v] … a horizontal line" interruption and repair example (p. 64).
text.formatted: We illustrate this principle with <ref type="bibr" target="#b123">Levelt's (1983)</ref> "… is a [v] … a horizontal line" interruption and repair example (p. 64).

text.text: The original utterance in Dutch was "… zit een [v] … een horizontale lijn." f horizontale was anticipated on the basis of MSPC, but verticale was ultimately spoken, the unfolding speech signal could provide cues to this mismatch before the onset of verticale.

Somatosensory cues could include, for example, movement of the lower lip toward the configuration for the labiodental /v/, rather than the lip-rounding associated with the upcoming /ɔ/ of horizontale, together with a more front/central rather than retracted tongue-body configuration.

Auditory consequences could include relatively higher F2 values during the preceding unstressed vowel, rather than the lower F2 expected from anticipation of /ɔ/, and comparatively less F3 lowering associated with lip rounding.
Thus, coarticulatory cues could potentially reveal, in real time, that the developing utterance is inconsistent with the speech event anticipated by MSPC.
Coarticulatory cues toward verticale need not generate a specific anticipation of verticale (although, given the constrained context in this particular case, such anticipation is possible).

Crucially, we therefore propose that the relevant contrast is not between coarticulation suggesting the utterance anticipated with MSPC (here horizontale) and anticipatory coarticulation suggesting the upcoming erroneous utterance (verticale)-rather, the relevant contrast is between horizontale and something sufficiently different from horizontale, signaling that what is anticipated is not what is about to be uttered.

We therefore suggest that withinword errors-such as the phonological anticipation errors "John dropped his cuff of coffee" or "alsho share" (Fromkin, 1971)-can be detected due to a contrast between MSPC-based anticipation and such within-word coarticulatory information.

text.text: As we have seen, not all detected errors lead to rapid interruptions.

We propose that rapid interruptions depend on specific preconditions: (a) that the relevant MSPC-based anticipation is distinct, clear, and unambiguous enough for divergent auditory and/or somatosensory information to provide a salient cue that the unfolding utterance is problematic; (b) that the utterance anticipated with MSPC and the utterance being produced differ in articulatory properties capable of generating distinct anticipatory somatosensory and/or auditory information; (c) that these differences are sufficiently expressed in the unfolding articulation to produce sensory information that diverges saliently from the MSPCbased anticipation (the extent of this divergence may vary, for example, with the degree to which different articulatory patterns are co-expressed in error segments and with how clearly the speaker enunciates); and (d) that the interruption implementation latency is sufficiently short.
An additional, less certain variable is (e) whether the speaker's attention is focused on their own speech.
However, the satisfaction of these preconditions does not guarantee that a rapid interruption will occur.
Specifically, detection latency need not map directly onto overt interruption latency.

Speakers sometimes hold off interrupting an error until a repair is ready (Seyfeddinipur et al., 2008), meaning that two errors-one detected rapidly through anticipatory mechanisms and one detected later through post-articulatory sensory feedback-could in principle have similar overt interruption latencies.

text.text: Beyond these preconditions, several linguistic, articulatory, and comprehensionbased factors are likely to contribute to variability in the interruption latency of errors detected through anticipatory processing.
First, the point at which useful anticipatory coarticulatory information becomes available differs across speech sounds and articulatory features (Lulaci et al., 2024; Schreiber & McMurray, 2019).

text.text: Second, speakers show variability in both the magnitude and temporal extent of coarticulation during speech, both between speakers (Lo et al., 2023; Perkell & Matthies, 1992) and within speakers across utterances (Perkell & Matthies, 1992).

text.text: As we saw above, anticipatory error detection may fail because the coarticulatory contrast between the anticipated and produced utterances is insufficiently large, or because the produced coarticulatory cues are insufficiently prominent to signal the divergence.

We propose that errors-including all the errors referenced in the previous section-can also be detected based on divergence between lexical or phonological activation generated by MSPC-based anticipation and activation generated through post-articulatory selfcomprehension via auditory and somatosensory feedback.
This route to error detection should generally result in slower interruption times because the relevant sensory information becomes available only after articulation.

While we propose that the most rapid error interruptions arise from MSPC-based and coarticulatory anticipation, the quicker interruptions resulting from divergence between MSPC-based anticipation and postarticulatory sensory feedback may nonetheless overlap temporally with the slower interruptions based on anticipatory coarticulatory cues.

Direct estimates of the processing times required to identify individual speech sounds in the absence of preceding coarticulatory cues are difficult to obtain. 11 Nonetheless, the studies reviewed above on the temporal advantage provided by coarticulatory cues offer some indirect constraints on lower-bound speech processing latencies.

text.text: Finally, we suggest that speech errors can be detected through post-articulatory selfcomprehension in the absence of sufficiently informative prior anticipation.

Post-articulatory speech input will, as we saw above, generally provide stronger activation than anticipatory information based on MSPC (Falandays et al., 2021) or coarticulation (Schreiber & McMurray, 2019).

text.text: We suggested that post-articulatory auditory feedback is similarly the strongest cue for self-comprehension.

While anticipatory self-comprehension based on MSPC and coarticulation can sometimes provide enough information to elicit rapid error detection, it is unlikely to provide speakers with as comprehensive an understanding of the meaning and consequences of their utterances as post-articulatory self-comprehension.

We therefore suggest that self-comprehension in the wider sense of understanding and contextualizing one's utterances within a given communicative situation-something that is more time-consuming-is likely to depend particularly strongly on post-articulatory information.

Similarly, to achieve self-comprehension in general, including the detection of errors (especially appropriateness errors), integration-that is, the linking of current linguistic input with prior context and general background knowledge (e.g., Abashidze et al., 2019; Ferreira & Chantavarin, 2018)-is likely to be crucial alongside anticipation.

text.text: More broadly, spoken communication is ultimately directed toward the communication and comprehension of meaning rather than merely phonological or lexical processing (see Meekings & Scott, 2025), and we suggest that this is also true for the selfcomprehending speaker.

text.text: During post-articulatory self-comprehension, the emphasis is likely to be on auditory feedback and the broader contextual information, meaning that this form of self-comprehension is most similar to other-comprehension (but it is not identical, as we will detail in a section below).
The characteristics of the three routes to self-comprehension and self-monitoring discussed above lead to several predictions concerning error detection patterns and timings.
Post-articulatory self-comprehension should, as a rule, result in longer error-interruption latencies than self-comprehension based on anticipatory information.

Speakers can likely detect all error types through post-articulatory self-comprehension, but this mechanism should generally not support the very rapid error detection and interruption enabled by the anticipatory routes.

In fact, given the uncertain and incomplete nature of anticipatory speech processing via MSPC and coarticulation, many errors, regardless of error type, should be detected through post-articulatory self-comprehension.
At the same time, there is likely to be a difference in interruption latency between appropriateness and production-based errors.
The problems triggering appropriateness repairs should be considerably easier to detect through post-articulatory than anticipatory self-comprehension.

Production-based speech errors, by contrast, will often-but, as we have seen, not always-provide a clearer contrast with MSPC-based anticipation at the phonological and lexical levels and should therefore be more likely than appropriateness errors to be detected rapidly through anticipatory selfcomprehension.

Additionally, appropriateness errors should show greater variability in interruption latency, both because they will primarily be detected by contextualizing the utterance through post-articulatory self-comprehension and because the locus of the problem will often be less clearly defined than for production-based errors.

These predictions are consistent with the available data on interruption timing. Levelt (1983) reported that a majority of both production-based repairs (308 of 399, 77%) and appropriateness repairs (270 of 290, 93%) were interrupted at some point after the troublesome word.

Nonetheless, the strong influence of post-articulatory auditory feedback that we have proposed suggests that the auditory feedback of green may often dominate this anticipatory and somatosensory information.

The self-comprehension theory proposes that the relative weighting of different anticipatory and post-articulatory cues may vary from utterance to utterance, for example depending on how strongly the available contextual constraints influence processing and on the prominence-in both somatosensory and auditory feedback-of coarticulatory cues.
This suggests that variability along several dimensions-both from trial to trial and between participants-may contribute to variation in whether the manipulation is detected.

Specifically, within-word anticipatory coarticulatory information in the shared onset /gr/ should differ across sensory modalities: somatosensory coarticulatory information generated while producing gray should be consistent with the MSPC-based anticipation of gray, whereas auditory coarticulatory information in the inserted auditory feedback should be consistent with the subsequently arriving auditory information specifying green.

When sufficiently prominent, this cross-modal divergence could provide a cue to the manipulation, with variability in the realization and perceptual prominence of coarticulation potentially contributing to trial-to-trial and between-participant variability in detection.

Additional discrepancies associated more specifically with the record-and-playback methodology-such as temporal misalignment of the voice exchange or differences in the prosody or amplitude of the spoken and heard utterances-also vary from trial to trial and between participants and provide cues to the manipulation. Lind et al. (2014a) found that exchanges with less accurate temporal alignment between the produced and inserted words were substantially more likely to be detected, demonstrating that the degree of correspondence between produced and inserted speech can influence detection.

text.text: In this section, we detail Lackner and Tuller's (1979) data, including Levelt's (1989) influential interpretation of these findings, and show how they can be accounted for within the self-comprehension model without requiring a separate internal, pre-articulatory monitoring channel. Lackner and Tuller (1979) asked participants to repeat syllable sequences such as pi-di-ti-gi, ae-i-o-u, or pi-ae-ti-o, one sequence per second for 30 seconds each in two conditions: with normal auditory feedback and with auditory feedback masked by white noise.

text.text: Participants were instructed to press a button whenever they noticed that they made a speech error.

For consonant-vowel syllables, Lackner and Tuller (1979) found that when auditory feedback was masked, participants were somewhat less accurate in detecting place-of-articulation errors (e.g., saying [ti] instead of [pi]), but substantially worse at detecting voicing errors (e.g., saying [bi] instead of [pi]) than when auditory feedback was available.

text.text: For vowel syllables, noise masking substantially impaired detection of vowel-tovowel errors, whereas detection of vowel-to-consonant errors was much less affected.
Notably, however, this reduction in vowel-to-vowel error detection was concentrated primarily among errors involving small articulatory differences.
Vowel errors involving large articulatory differences were generally detected even under auditory masking.

Importantly, Lackner and Tuller (1979) also found that a slightly larger proportion of error-offset-to-button press latencies fell within the 0-50 ms range under auditory masking (2.3%) than with normal auditory feedback (0.4%). 14Lackner and Tuller (1979) proposed that speech errors can be detected by comparing corollary-discharge representations of intended speech with corollary-discharge signals from motor programming, and with auditory and proprioceptive feedback.

text.text: They argued that voicing errors during CV syllables and vowel errors involving small articulatory differences are detected primarily through auditory feedback, whereas under noise masking, detection of place-of-articulation errors for CV syllables and of vowel errors involving larger articulatory differences can draw more strongly on proprioceptive information.

They further proposed that the rapid detections during both normal and noise-masked speech indicate additional monitoring via corollary-discharge information (as we saw above, Lackner & Tuller, 1979, assumed that overt use of somatosensory and auditory feedback requires a latency of 300-400 ms). text.text: He further argued that, under noise masking, the slower external loop is suspended, leaving detection to the internal loop.

In the self-comprehension model, we suggest that somatosensory feedback-not pre-articulatory monitoring of a phonetic (Levelt, 1989) or phonological (Wheeldon & Levelt, 1995) code-is relied upon during noise masking (for a related proposal concerning somatosensory and proprioceptive feedback, see also Nooteboom & Quené, 2017).

text.text: As discussed above, anticipatory coarticulation can provide somatosensory information about upcoming speech (Floegel et al., 2023; Kasper et al., 2026).

text.text: Crucially, rather than proposing that this feedback is compared with a representation of the intended utterance, we suggest that divergence between somatosensory feedback and MSPC-based anticipation can provide a cue that the unfolding utterance is problematic.
Errors may also be detected through post-articulatory self-comprehension based on somatosensory feedback in the absence of sufficiently informative prior anticipation.

However, contrary to Lackner and Tuller's (1979) proposal, the self-comprehension model suggests that the quicker detections may be based on anticipatory coarticulatory information, with both auditory and somatosensory feedback contributing during normal speech, and somatosensory feedback becoming particularly important under noise masking.

text.text: Thus, whereas Postma and Kolk (1992) noted that acoustic coarticulatory cues would be strongly, and perhaps completely, diminished by noise masking, we extend the possibility they raised for verbal self-monitoring to somatosensory coarticulatory information, which remains available when auditory feedback is masked.

text.text: We suggest that the distribution of button-press latencies can be understood in the same way as the broader distribution reviewed above (Blackmer & Mitton, 1991; Hartsuiker & Kolk, 2001; Levelt, 1983): the most rapid detections may rely on anticipatory coarticulatory information, whereas progressively longer latencies may reflect increasing reliance on post-articulatory feedback. text.text: However, two issues complicate this interpretation.
First, the proportion of button presses within 50 ms was very low (0.4% with normal feedback and 2.3% with noise masking).

Second, and critically, error-to-button-press latency in Lackner and Tuller's (1979) first experiment was measured from error offset rather than error onset (the error-to-cutoff times reported by Blackmer & Mitton, 1991, and Hartsuiker & Kolk, 2001, were measured from error onset).
text.formatted: Second, and critically, error-to-button-press latency in <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">Lackner and Tuller's (1979)</ref> first experiment was measured from error offset rather than error onset (the error-to-cutoff times reported by <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Blackmer &</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Mitton, 1991, and</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Hartsuiker &</ref> <ref type="bibr">Kolk, 2001</ref>, were measured from error onset).

text.text: Consequently, these offset-based latencies provide no direct estimate of how long after error onset the button press occurred and therefore cannot establish that the responses in the 0-50 ms interval reflected exceptionally rapid error detection.
Moreover, relating these offset-based latencies to error onset requires knowing how long the erroneous production lasted, and we do not know how much of each error was spoken.

Although the instructions were to produce each four-syllable sequence over one second, it is difficult to keep a precise rhythm, meaning that individual syllable durations were unlikely to be fixed at exactly 250 ms.
Furthermore, some erroneous syllables may have been interrupted before completion.

In a second experiment, described in detail below, Lackner and Tuller (1979) measured error-to-button press latencies from both error onset and offset; for self-produced errors, the mean difference between these measures was 186 ms.

text.text: Using this as an approximate guide, a button press occurring 0-50 ms after error offset in the first experiment would correspond to roughly 186-236 ms after error onset.

Taken together, these considerations mean that the higher proportion of button presses occurring 0-50 ms after error offset under noise masking does not establish exceptionally rapid error detection under masking, nor does it establish that errors were detected more rapidly under masking than with normal auditory feedback. text.text: However, a methodological issue complicates interpretation of the data.

To create the speech-perception stimuli, Lackner and Tuller (1979) spliced recordings of syllables into the same sequences as in the production task, with errors created by occasionally splicing in an incorrect syllable (e.g., /ti/ instead of /pi/).
text.formatted: To create the speech-perception stimuli, <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">Lackner and Tuller (1979)</ref> spliced recordings of syllables into the same sequences as in the production task, with errors created by occasionally splicing in an incorrect syllable (e.g., /ti/ instead of /pi/).

text.text: This means that the perception stimuli lacked the naturally produced anticipatory information extending from the preceding speech into the erroneous syllable that could have been present in naturalistic continuous speech.
In the production task, by contrast, anticipatory coarticulatory information was potentially available through somatosensory feedback.

We therefore suggest that the observed reaction-time difference cannot be taken as a straightforward estimate of the difference between error detection during natural speech perception and production.
16   In summary, the self-comprehension model provides an account of error detection under noise-masked auditory feedback that does not require a separate pre-articulatory monitoring channel.

If self-monitoring does not rely on privileged access to internal representations specifying upcoming speech-and if speakers do not, for example, have access to an internal monitoring channel (e.g., Levelt, 1989), to predictions based on the intention (e.g., Pickering & Garrod, 2013), or to conflict in the production system (Nozari et al., 2011)-does this mean that self-comprehension is essentially identical to other-comprehension?
text.formatted: If self-monitoring does not rely on privileged access to internal representations specifying upcoming speech-and if speakers do not, for example, have access to an internal monitoring channel (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b124">Levelt, 1989)</ref>, to predictions based on the intention (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b192">Pickering & Garrod, 2013)</ref>, or to conflict in the production system <ref type="bibr" target="#b176">(Nozari et al., 2011)</ref>-does this mean that self-comprehension is essentially identical to other-comprehension?

text.text: We suggest that this is not so, and that self-comprehension is at least partly distinct from othercomprehension, for at least five reasons.
First, during self-comprehension, but not during other-comprehension, the speaker has access to speech-production-related motor information and somatosensory feedback.

Anticipatory coarticulation also generates somatosensory information that is available only to the speaker, providing a source of information about upcoming speech that listeners-who can exploit auditory but not somatosensory coarticulatory cues from the speaker-do not possess.
16 It is nevertheless plausible that reaction times would differ between the two tasks even if naturalistic stimuli were used in the perception task.

As we discuss in the section The Special Status of Self-Comprehension Distinguishes It from Other-Comprehension below, self-comprehension is unlikely to be identical to othercomprehension for several reasons, including the availability of somatosensory feedback.
The magnitude of any reaction-time difference between production and perception, however, remains an empirical question.
self-vocalization but not playback, indicating that the peripheral auditory state through which self-produced speech will subsequently be processed can already differ before the speech signal begins.

Thus, before listeners receive the first acoustic information from an utterance, the speaker already differs from the listener both in the production-related motor and somatosensory information available and in the state of the auditory system through which the ensuing speech signal will be processed.
We hypothesize that these pre-acoustic production-related states can contribute to the distinctive processing conditions of selfcomprehension.

Fourth, the contextual information constraining comprehension may differ in richness and specificity depending on the speaker. Ryskin et al. (2020) demonstrated that listeners can use contextual knowledge about a specific speaker to constrain anticipation of that speaker's upcoming speech.
