(2020)</ref> demonstrated that listeners can use contextual knowledge about a specific speaker to constrain anticipation of that speaker's upcoming speech.

text.text: Within an MSPC account, such talker-specific knowledge could contribute to differences in the precision of anticipations across speakers.
In particular, the speaker has an exceptionally rich history of self-specific linguistic, conceptual, and contextual regularities that could constrain comprehension of their own speech.

Consistent with the possibility that self-specific knowledge can facilitate anticipation, Hadley et al. (2020) found that listeners predicted turn endings more precisely when the speaker's speech style was more similar to their own.
text.formatted: Consistent with the possibility that self-specific knowledge can facilitate anticipation, <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Hadley et al. (2020)</ref> found that listeners predicted turn endings more precisely when the speaker's speech style was more similar to their own.

text.text: Thus, unlike the speaker-exclusive sensory information described above, talker-specific contextual information need not be unique to selfcomprehension, but it may nevertheless provide richer constraints when comprehending one's own speech.

Finally, the speaker, but not the listener, has experiential access to whatever inner experiences (e.g., Hurlburt & Heavey, 2006)-including inner speech (e.g., Hurlburt et al., 2013; Hurlburt & Heavey, 2018) and inner visual imagery (Heavey & Hurlburt, 2008)-might precede, coincide with, or follow overt speech (Linell, 2009, pp. 122-130; Linell, 2024).
text.formatted: Finally, the speaker, but not the listener, has experiential access to whatever inner experiences (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">Hurlburt & Heavey, 2006</ref>)-including inner speech (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b94">Hurlburt et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">Hurlburt & Heavey, 2018)</ref> and inner visual imagery <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">(Heavey & Hurlburt, 2008)</ref>-might precede, coincide with, or follow overt speech <ref type="bibr">(Linell, 2009, pp. 122-130;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b136">Linell, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Such inner experiences should not, however, be equated with speech intentions or with conceptual representations specifying the content of an utterance.
Neither should they be equated with the contents of an internal monitoring channel or with other internal representations of upcoming speech.
They may nevertheless be related to overt speech in a variety of ways and could therefore contribute to the contextual state constraining MSPC during self-comprehension.
At present, however, very little is known about these relationships.

We consider these relationships further in Lind et al. (2026) and investigate them empirically during spontaneous speech using descriptive experience sampling (Hurlburt & Heavey, 2006; Lind & Hermansson, 2026).

text.text: Taken together, these differences suggest that self-comprehension operates on a richer and partly distinct set of sensory, motor, contextual, and experiential information than other-comprehension.
Several observations at the cortical level have been interpreted as evidence for predictive processing during verbal self-monitoring.

First, neural responses, particularly in auditory cortex, are often reduced during speaking relative to passive playback of matched self-produced speech, a phenomenon commonly termed speaking-induced suppression (SIS; e.g., Chang et al., 2013; Curio et al., 2000; Gonzalez et al., 2024; Greenlee et al., 2011; Heinks-Maldonado et al., 2005 , 2006; Kort et al., 2014; Kurteff et al., 2023; Ozker et al., 2024; Ventura et al., 2009; see Whitford, 2019, for review).

text.text: SIS and perturbation-related enhancement have consequently been taken as evidence for forward modeling and, more generally, predictive processing during speech.

Predictive mechanisms have further been proposed to contribute to speakers' ability to source-monitor-that is, to distinguish self-produced from externally produced speech (e.g., Ford & Mathalon, 2005; Ford et al., 2007; Heinks-Maldonado et al., 2005; Heinks-Maldonado et al., 2007; Houde & Nagarajan, 2011; Houde et al., 2002)-and to the sense of agency over their own utterances (e.g., Ohata et al., 2022; Sugimori et al., 2011).

text.text: Sensory attenuation should therefore not, by itself, be treated as a proxy for prediction.

Related concerns about inferring prediction from action-related auditory attenuation have been raised by Horváth (2015), who reviewed evidence that auditory attenuation can occur even in the absence of a contingent action-sound relationship.

text.text: A related interpretive problem applies to both SIS and SPRE, which are defined by differences in auditory-cortical responses between speaking and passive-playback conditions.
Such contrasts cannot by themselves identify which of the multiple differences between sensory processing during speaking and playback gives rise to the observed cortical effects.

More specifically, the vocalization-related changes in middle-ear function demonstrated by Terband et al. (2024), including stronger reflex activation during self-vocalization than during listening, provide a concrete peripheral mechanism relevant to SIS.
text.formatted: More specifically, the vocalization-related changes in middle-ear function demonstrated by <ref type="bibr" target="#b234">Terband et al. (2024)</ref>, including stronger reflex activation during self-vocalization than during listening, provide a concrete peripheral mechanism relevant to SIS.

text.text: Because the middle-ear muscle reflex reduces low-frequency input to the cochlea, part of the cortical attenuation measured as SIS could arise from differences in auditory input already present at the auditory periphery.
More generally, the neuroimaging evidence for cortical auditory-feedback error-monitoring mechanisms is itself inconclusive.

In a systematic review and metaanalysis, Meekings and Scott (2021) concluded that the available fMRI and PET evidence was insufficient to establish that the posterior superior gyrus functions as an error monitor during speech production.

text.text: Taken together, these considerations caution against treating cortical attenuation and perturbation-related responses as uniquely diagnostic of the predictive error-monitoring mechanisms proposed by forward models, while leaving open the possibility that at least some attenuation associated with speaking reflects peripheral and more general action-dependent modulation of sensory processing rather than predictive cancellation.
A similar interpretive issue arises in language comprehension, where reduced neural responses to expected input have often been taken as evidence for prediction.

For example, semantically unexpected words, such as dog in I take coffee with cream and dog, elicit an enhanced N400 compared with expected completions such as sugar, during both reading (e.g., Kutas & Hillyard, 1980 , 1984) and listening (Friederici et al., 1993; Hagoort & Brown, 2000; Holcomb & Neville, 1991).

text.text: As we have seen, TRACE does not explicitly represent predictions, but its interactive activation dynamics can produce anticipatory activation of phonemes that have not yet been encountered.
Crucially, Luthra et al. (2021) found lower activity at both lexical and phoneme levels when the input was expected.
text.formatted: Crucially, <ref type="bibr" target="#b142">Luthra et al. (2021)</ref> found lower activity at both lexical and phoneme levels when the input was expected.

text.text: In TRACE, unexpected input is compatible with more lexical competitors, producing greater aggregate activity and top-down feedback.

Thus, TRACE produces reduced activation for expected input without explicitly generating a prediction and computing the discrepancy between that prediction and the incoming signal (see also Falandays et al., 2021; Ryskin & Nieuwland, 2023). Luthra et al.'s (2021) demonstration therefore provides a computational example of a broader point: reduced activation for expected input need not uniquely identify an explicit predictive computation (see also Aitchison & Lengyel, 2017).

text.text: Together with Falandays et al.'s (2021) demonstration that anticipatory processing can emerge through multi-scale pattern completion without explicit representations of predictions or prediction errors, this raises the possibility that both anticipatory activation and reduced activation for expected input can emerge from the dynamics of an interactive pattern-completion system.

text.text: We propose that the same possibility should be considered for cortical attenuation during self-produced speech.

When a speaker prepares to produce an utterance-or to continue an ongoing utterance-MSPC may constrain the processing of concurrent and forthcoming sensory information on the basis of the evolving linguistic and contextual state, with the additional sensory, motor, contextual, and other information available during selfcomprehension providing additional constraints.

As discussed above, these constraints can include anticipatory auditory and somatosensory information generated by coarticulation, which may become informative about upcoming speech before the relevant segment itself is produced.

We propose that, by analogy with the TRACE dynamics demonstrated by Luthra et al. (2021), auditory input that is consistent with an already constrained processing state may require less additional activation than input encountered in a less constrained state.
text.formatted: We propose that, by analogy with the TRACE dynamics demonstrated by <ref type="bibr" target="#b142">Luthra et al. (2021)</ref>, auditory input that is consistent with an already constrained processing state may require less additional activation than input encountered in a less constrained state.

text.text: During speaking, auditory feedback is processed within the evolving, multimodally constrained state characteristic of self-comprehension, including MSPC-based constraints together with the production-related sensory, motor, and contextual information described above.

During passive playback, MSPC can likewise constrain processing on the basis of the unfolding linguistic and communicative context, although the particular constraints available to MSPC need not be identical across speaking and playback.

More importantly, the same acoustic signal is encountered without the same combination and temporal configuration of sensory, motor, contextual, and other constraints available during ongoing self-comprehension.
The same acoustic input could therefore elicit less auditory-cortical activity during speaking than during playback, producing SIS without requiring predictive cancellation.

This account is also compatible with the observation that suppression is sensitive to the correspondence between produced and heard speech (e.g., Heinks-Maldonado et al., 2005; Heinks-Maldonado et al., 2006): feedback that is less consistent with the evolving state should recruit more additional processing than feedback that is consistent with it.
text.formatted: This account is also compatible with the observation that suppression is sensitive to the correspondence between produced and heard speech (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Heinks-Maldonado et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Heinks-Maldonado et al., 2006)</ref>: feedback that is less consistent with the evolving state should recruit more additional processing than feedback that is consistent with it.

text.text: Crucially, this account does not require that a detailed auditory representation first be generated as an explicit prediction and subsequently compared with the incoming signal.

A similar, although more tentative, argument can be made for perturbation-related enhancement. Luthra et al. (2021) directly demonstrate an alternative explanation for attenuation rather than SPRE, and sensorimotor-gating accounts have likewise primarily targeted sensory attenuation rather than perturbation enhancement.
text.formatted: A similar, although more tentative, argument can be made for perturbation-related enhancement. <ref type="bibr" target="#b142">Luthra et al. (2021)</ref> directly demonstrate an alternative explanation for attenuation rather than SPRE, and sensorimotor-gating accounts have likewise primarily targeted sensory attenuation rather than perturbation enhancement.

text.text: Nevertheless, enhanced responses to unexpected input need not imply an explicitly computed prediction error: in TRACE, for example, unexpected input produces greater activation because it engages a larger set of competing representations, rather than because the system computes a discrepancy between a sensory prediction and its outcome.
As proposed above, naturally occurring coarticulatory cues that diverge from MSPC-based anticipation may signal a developing speech error.
Experimentally perturbed auditory feedback may similarly provide sensory information that is inconsistent with the evolving MSPC-and sensoryconstrained state.

Such perturbations could therefore recruit additional processing, potentially contributing to the heightened cortical responses observed during speaking, without requiring comparison against an explicitly generated auditory prediction.
Cortical attenuation and perturbation-related enhancement are therefore compatible with predictive processing but do not, by themselves, establish an explicit predictive mechanism.

The concept of self-comprehension refers to speakers using feedback from their own speech in conjunction with wider contextual information to understand the meaning and significance of their own speech without assuming access to well-defined pre-articulatory speech representations.

We have proposed that verbal self-monitoring can be understood as a natural sub-function of self-comprehension, rather than as a dedicated process that evaluates the unfolding utterance against information derived from pre-articulatory representations.

In our model, speakers determine what they are saying, and whether it is erroneous or otherwise problematic, through a cue-integrative process in which contextual, linguistic, motor, and sensory information jointly constrain the interpretation of their unfolding speech.

Two sources of anticipatory information are particularly important: anticipation based on multi-scale pattern completion (MSPC; Falandays et al., 2021) and anticipation based on auditory and somatosensory information generated through coarticulation.
text.formatted: Two sources of anticipatory information are particularly important: anticipation based on multi-scale pattern completion (MSPC; <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Falandays et al., 2021)</ref> and anticipation based on auditory and somatosensory information generated through coarticulation.

text.text: When these sources of information support sufficiently divergent states, that divergence can provide a cue that the unfolding utterance is problematic, without requiring either an intended-utterance representation or a separate comparator mechanism.

Depending on which information is available and when it becomes informative, error detection may therefore arise through interactions between MSPC and anticipatory coarticulatory information, between MSPC and post-articulatory sensory feedback, or exclusively through post-articulatory self-comprehension in the wider linguistic and communicative context.

These routes should, on average, be associated with progressively longer but substantially overlapping error-interruption latencies, and could in principle accommodate the observed distribution of interruption latencies-including differences in the prevalence and interruption latencies of different error types-without requiring privileged monitoring access to internal production representations specifying upcoming speech.

On this account, verbal selfmonitoring does not require a dedicated monitoring system with privileged access to speechproduction representations; instead, monitoring emerges as part of the speaker's ongoing comprehension of their own speech.
While we have presented MSPC and anticipatory coarticulatory information as intimately intertwined, their respective contributions to verbal self-comprehension could also be evaluated separately.
MSPC provides a reconceptualization of anticipatory phenomena commonly interpreted as evidence for explicit prediction during speech comprehension (Falandays et al., 2021).

text.text: More generally, however, MSPC illustrates how anticipatory processing might emerge without explicit representations of future states or computations of prediction error.

Importantly, the proposed contribution of anticipatory coarticulatory information to self-comprehension does not depend on MSPC, or indeed on any particular account of how context-based anticipation is implemented.

Even if errors are in fact detected against clearly specified pre-articulatory information, speakers could nonetheless exploit coarticulation in unfolding sensory feedback to obtain anticipatory information about what is about to be uttered (Floegel et al., 2023; Kasper et al., 2026).

text.text: We extend this The present model concerns how erroneous or otherwise troublesome speech can be detected by the speaker; it does not presently attempt to explain how such speech arises during speech production.

More generally, because the model does not posit a fixed prearticulatory standard against which an unfolding utterance is judged, it raises the question of what makes an utterance an 'error' in the first place.

On the present account, error status emerges from the integration of sensory information about the unfolding utterance with the anticipatory, linguistic, and communicative constraints available during self-comprehension.
On this view, an error need not be defined solely by deviation from a single internally represented intended utterance.

What counts as problematic can depend on multiple constraints, including linguistic well-formedness, the developing interpretation of the utterance, the communicative context, and the responses of an interlocutor.

A fuller account of how these constraints determine error status lies beyond the present model, which concerns primarily how cues that the unfolding utterance is problematic can give rise to error detection.
The present account lends itself to several direct empirical tests.
We give three examples.

First, a sufficiently large corpus of spontaneous speech errors recorded with highfidelity audio could test whether the prominence, onset, and temporal extent of anticipatory acoustic coarticulation predict error interruption latency, particularly in relation to contextual constraint.

Second, using RSE (Lind et al., 2014a (Lind et al., , 2014b)), the contribution of within-word anticipatory coarticulatory information in real-time auditory feedback could be manipulated through cross-splicing (Beddor et al., 2013; Dahan et al., 2001).
text.formatted: Second, using RSE <ref type="bibr">(Lind et al., 2014a</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b129">(Lind et al., , 2014b))</ref>, the contribution of within-word anticipatory coarticulatory information in real-time auditory feedback could be manipulated through cross-splicing <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Beddor et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Dahan et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: In a task where participants are instructed to interrupt utterances when the feedback relays a different word from the one they are producing, would they interrupt an utterance of, for example, best while hearing bend more rapidly when the feedback contains the natural anticipatory coarticulatory cues of bend than when its initial vowel material is cross-spliced from best?

Finally, the contribution of somatosensory feedback-including anticipatory coarticulatory information-could be tested by extending Lackner and Tuller's (1979) auditory-masking paradigm with conditions in which oral somatosensation is disrupted through local anesthesia (see, e.g., De Letter et al., 2020).

text.text: In summary, the self-comprehension model shifts the explanatory problem of verbal self-monitoring.

Rather than asking how speakers compare what they say with a prearticulatory representation specifying what they intended to say, it asks how speakers determine what they are saying-and whether it is problematic-from the evolving information available during speaking.
On this view, monitoring is not a separate inspection of speech production, but an emergent consequence of making sense of one's own unfolding speech.

text.text: More importantly for self-comprehension, the sensory signal available during speaking differs from that available when listening to another speaker.

Whereas listeners receive an interlocutor's voice primarily through air conduction, speakers perceive their own voice-beyond somatosensory feedback-through a combination of air-and bone/soft tissue conduction together with associated vibrotactile information (e.g., Orepic et al., 2023; Orepic & Pinheiro, 2026; Reinfeldt et al., 2010; Reinfeldt et al., 2013; Shuster & Durrant, 2003).

text.text: The auditory signal available during self-produced speech is further modulated by activation of the middleear muscles during vocalization, which alters transmission to the cochlea and attenuates particularly low-frequency components of self-generated sound (Schneider et al., 2018; Terband et al., 2024; Ugarteburu et al., 2022).

text.text: Thus, even at relatively peripheral levels of sensory processing, the information available for comprehending one's own ongoing speech differs from that available for comprehending another person's speech.
Third, speech-production-related information becomes available to the speaker before the onset of audible speech.

Articulatory, respiratory, and laryngeal activity can begin tens or even hundreds of milliseconds before acoustic onset (e.g., Cavallo & Baken, 1985; Jouen et al., 2021; Kawamoto et al., 2008; McFarland, 2001; McFarland & Smith, 1992; Tilsen et al., 2016), and speech-related readiness-potential and motor-preparation activity likewise precedes speech onset (e.g., Brumberg et al., 2015; Wohlert, 1993).

text.text: Applied to self-comprehension, this raises the possibility that MSPC and coarticulatory information are not temporally isolated sources of anticipation.

Rather, sensory information from the unfolding utterance may contribute to the evolving context within which subsequent pattern completion occurs, while MSPC-based anticipation may simultaneously constrain the processing of that sensory information.

Although we have focused on coarticulation, other sources of anticipatory sensory information-particularly in the acoustic modality-could similarly constrain processing of upcoming speech and potentially contribute to the detection of errors and other problems during self-comprehension.

For example, various prosodic cues have been demonstrated to support forward anticipation during other-comprehension, including prosodic structure (e.g., Nakamura et al., 2012; Weber et al., 2006b), contrastive pitch accent (e.g., Ito & Speer, 2008; Ito et al., 2012; Weber et al., 2006a), and Swedish word accents (Kwon & Roll, 2024).

text.text: Coarticulation should therefore be understood as one particularly well-documented source of anticipatory sensory information rather than as the only possible sensory route through which the unfolding utterance can constrain self-comprehension in advance of later speech events.

text.text: Articulatory coarticulation is not invariably accompanied by an equally detectable acoustic effect(Butcher & Weiher, 1976; Recasens et al., 1997), raising the possibility that somatosensory information generated by anticipatory coarticulation may sometimes become informative earlier than, or be more informative than, the corresponding auditory information (seeKasper et al., 2026).
